sections.heading: Title
sections.source_text: Tabular language models promise to unlock the mountains of spreadsheets sitting inside industrial companies, but they need labeled data, and only scarce domain experts can annotate the highly technical tables. This paper, presented at the Table Representation Learning Workshop at NeurIPS 2022 by Martin Ringsquandl and Aneta Koleva from Siemens, asks a simple question: can active learning cut that labeling cost? They study sub-cell named entity recognition on a real industrial dataset and compare acquisition functions that pick which cells an expert should label next. The headline finding is that a batch-diverse gradient method called BADGE reaches full-training performance with far fewer labels, while forcing maximum table diversity actually hurts.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.source_text: Industry runs on spreadsheets. Plant operators track equipment, sensors, and vessels in loosely structured tables, and extracting that information automatically requires fine-tuning tabular language models on labeled examples. The catch is cost: these tables use highly technical, domain-specific language that only a handful of experts can annotate, so acquiring enough labels quickly becomes prohibitively expensive. The paper frames this as a sub-cell named entity recognition task and observes that it is a genuinely new kind of active learning problem, because each table contains many cells and each cell contains multiple token-level labels at once.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.source_text: Active learning is built exactly for situations with plentiful unlabeled data and expensive labels: it tries to squeeze the most model performance out of every annotation. But large transformer models can't be updated one example at a time; they need batches trained over several epochs, which means the acquisition function must pick a whole batch at once. Pure uncertainty sampling tends to grab very similar, correlated cells, often from the same table or even the same row, wasting the annotation budget. Despite this obvious fit, the authors point out that no one had yet studied active learning together with tabular language models, which is the gap they set out to fill.

sections.heading: Method
sections.source_text: The model is a tabular language model: a transformer encoder that replaces vanilla attention with a row-column visibility matrix and uses within-cell positional encoding, so each token gets a representation aware of the whole table. A classification decoder then labels every token with IO tags over four entity types: equipment tags, equipment names, physical quantities, and units of measurement. On top of this sits pool-based active learning, which repeatedly picks a batch of the most informative cells for an expert oracle to label. The authors compare four acquisition functions. MNLP scores cells by their normalized log-probability uncertainty. MNLP+ adds a forced round-robin across tables to maximize table diversity. BADGE clusters per-cell gradient embeddings with k-means++ to get a batch that is both uncertain and diverse. And Rand simply samples cells uniformly at random as a baseline.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.source_text: The evaluation uses a real industrial dataset, not an academic benchmark. Spreadsheets from several plants were downsampled so that each table had at most five rows, and expert annotators labeled every cell using the prodi.gy span-based annotation tool. After a random train-test split, there are 55 tables for training and 24 for testing. The training set contains 4,774 cells but only about 1,100 entity labels, which works out to just 0.23 labels per cell. That means roughly 77 percent of cells contain no entity at all, an extreme class imbalance that the authors note is very typical of real industrial data.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.source_text: The central result is measured by micro-averaged F1 on the held-out test set across active learning iterations. BADGE, the batch-diverse gradient method, is the standout: it clearly outperforms random selection and even surpasses the ceiling set by training on the full dataset, all while using far fewer labels. Pure uncertainty sampling with MNLP is disappointing, only pulling slightly ahead of random after around 500 labels, and with noticeably higher variance that signals sensitivity to the initial seed. Most striking, the MNLP+ variant that forces maximum table diversity is the worst of all, showing that pushing diversity too hard actively hurts.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.source_text: The four acquisition functions effectively ablate the role of diversity. Comparing them shows that the right amount of diversity matters enormously. BADGE's built-in batch diversity is beneficial, but MNLP+'s forced maximum table diversity is harmful, falling below even random sampling. To understand why, the authors track how many distinct tables each method draws cells from at each iteration. MNLP fixates on just a few tables, MNLP+ spreads across as many as the budget permits, and BADGE strikes a balance in the middle. This confirms that the goal is not maximum diversity but a careful trade-off between diversity and per-cell uncertainty.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.source_text: The lasting message is that active learning really can slash the expert-labeling cost of tabular language models, but only if diversity is handled with care. Cell-level acquisition that builds in batch diversity, as BADGE does, reaches full-training performance with a fraction of the labels, whereas bluntly forcing maximum table diversity backfires and does worse than random. The winning recipe is to balance diversity against uncertainty rather than maximize either alone. As the first work on this problem, it also flags two open frontiers: the computational cost of table-diverse acquisition, and the extra cognitive load it places on the human annotators who must interpret each new table.
